headline: Creates a National Computer Forensics Institute under the Secret Service and authorizes DOJ training grants to help police and prosecutors handle cyber and white collar crime.
what_it_does: The law sets up a National Computer Forensics Institute inside the U.S. Secret Service for fiscal years 2017 through 2022. The institute trains and equips state, local, tribal, and territorial police, prosecutors, and judges to investigate cyber and electronic crimes, examine computers and phones as evidence, respond to network intrusions, and handle digital evidence in court. It may also provide qualifying officers with computer equipment, software, and tools, and it can expand the Secret Service's Electronic Crime Task Forces. Separately, it lets the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Assistance fund training and technical help for officers, investigators, auditors, and prosecutors who handle white collar crime, including high-tech, economic, and internet-based crimes against children.

who_it_affects.group: State, local, tribal, and territorial police officers
who_it_affects.how: They can receive federally funded training and, in some cases, computer equipment and software for cyber and electronic crime investigations.

who_it_affects.group: State, local, tribal, and territorial prosecutors and judges
who_it_affects.how: They can receive training on digital evidence, cyber crime, and related court challenges through the institute.

who_it_affects.group: Members of the Secret Service's Electronic Crime Task Forces
who_it_affects.how: The network of task forces may expand to include officers trained at the institute.

who_it_affects.group: Auditors and investigators who work on white collar crime
who_it_affects.how: They may receive federally funded training and technical help from the Justice Department to identify, investigate, and prosecute these crimes.

when_it_takes_effect: Upon enactment on November 2, 2017; the institute's authorization covers fiscal years 2017 through 2022.
